title: Pageflip access clustering lab notes
content:
Summary:
This is a lab-diary style investigation into a recurring long-tail latency phenomenon we observed across several LRU-backed KV cache hosts. We call the observed behavior a "pageflip": a rapid, correlated residency churn where a working set cluster shifts and previously warm pages get ejected, producing a transient period of heavy NVMe reads and p99/p999 latency spikes.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture measurement methodology and synthetic workloads used to reproduce the pageflip.
- Record observed signals (reuse rate drop, NVMe throughput, PCIe saturation proxy, token latency distributions).
- Sketch hypotheses and low-risk mitigations to A/B.
- Proposed next experiments and owners.

Context / how we saw it:
- Triggered by a customer workload mix change: small burst of long-seq summarization requests overlapping with many short-turn chat requests.
- Symptoms: median token latency increases modestly, but p99 and p999 explode for ~30–90s windows on affected VMs.
- Console traces show concurrent NVMe read spikes and a sharp drop in per-request KV reuse.

Repro methodology (lab):
1) Two synthetic clients: "chat-short" (seqlen ~ 40, high QPS) and "doc-long" (seqlen ~ 1200, low QPS).
2) Start steady-state with chat-short for 5 minutes to build warm residency. Reuse_rate ~78% measured at host-level telemetry.
3) Inject doc-long workload (burst of 60 requests over 20s) and continue chat-short concurrently.
4) Sample resident-set snapshots every 10s, collect per-request KV hit/miss, NVMe op counters, PCIe link util (derived), and per-token latency.
5) Repeat with different mixes (1:0.1, 1:0.5, 1:1 doc:chat ratios).

Key observed numbers (lab run #7, representative):
- Baseline reuse rate (chat-only): 78% (std 3%).
- During pageflip window: reuse rate drops to 36% (min 28%).
- Host NVMe read throughput peak: 3.8 GB/s (sustained ~12s during worst window).
- Estimated PCIe bandwidth proxy shows ~85% utilization at peak.
- Median token latency: 12 ms -> 32 ms during window. p95: 42 ms -> 180 ms. p99: 115 ms -> 420 ms. p999: 210 ms -> 1.8 s.
- CPU: no obvious CPU saturation on host (user+system < 45%).
- Writeback/compaction background jobs increased I/O scatter, correlating with the worst tails.

Micro-tracing notes:
- Resident-set delta analysis shows cluster migration: ~40% of hot keys shifted to different allocation stripes within a 15s interval.
- Read amplification: single logical KV read produced multiple small NVMe reads (4–12) depending on page alignment; small IO size increased latency per operation.
- Prefetch triggered inconsistently: when prefetch latency budget < 8ms we saw too-late arrivals and wasted bandwidth.

Interpretation / hypotheses (ordered by plausibility):
1) Access-clustering + eviction hysteresis mismatch: Our eviction aggressiveness is tuned for steady hotspots; a fast cluster shift causes eviction of recently used pages before the new cluster is fully resident, creating many cold misses.
2) Bank/stripe imbalance: Hot cluster mapped to a set of NVMe/PCIe lanes that temporarily saturate, causing queuing and amplified read latencies for small IOs.
3) Prefetch heuristics are conservative for mixed seqlen workloads, so we miss the opportunity to warm pages ahead when a long request touches many new pages in sequence.
4) Background maintenance (compaction, defrag) overlaps I/O window and raises effective I/O tail probability.
5) Small-IO amplification from page-alignment leading to high IOPS and poor per-op latency — exacerbated by kernel block layer and NVMe queues not coalescing small reads consistently.

Mitigations tried in lab (quick experiments):
- Increase eviction hysteresis window (+20s): reduced p99 by ~30% but increased steady-state memory pressure and occasional OOM-like reclaim events on smaller hosts.
- Pinning a tiny fraction of keys (top 3% by recent frequency) during the shift: reduced p999 by ~40% in these runs; operationally expensive to choose pins without false positives.
- Aggressive prefetch for long sequences (speculative prefetch ahead by 8 pages): reduced NVMe burst but increased overall bandwidth usage by ~22% (cost tradeoff).
- Throttle background compaction in windows where per-host NVMe throughput > 2.5 GB/s: reduced tails but deferred fragmentation work.

Why these results are interesting / tradeoffs:
- Hysteresis helps tails but increases resident memory and can reduce effective cache efficiency for other tenants.
- Speculative prefetch trades bandwidth/cost for latency; good for premium customers but not default.
- Pinning is effective but requires reliable hot-key detection and is brittle under sudden traffic changes.

Detection signals (for early mitigation):
- Rapid delta in per-request reuse rate (>20 percentage points drop within 10s).
- Spike in small-read NVMe ops (IO size distribution shifts left to <32KB median) concurrent with rising PCIe proxy.
- Sequence-length distribution skew shift: a sudden larger fraction of long-seq requests in sampling window.

Short-term proposals (low-risk, 2–4 weeks):
1) Implement a server-side detection trigger: if reuse_rate_delta > 20% && NVMe_read_rate > 2.0 GB/s for 5s, enable a temporary "warm-mode" that:
   - Increases eviction hysteresis by configurable factor (owner: Marco, PR: #3412).
   - Temporarily raises prefetch aggressiveness for currently active request contexts (owner: Lina).
2) Add more granular NVMe read histograms to our telemetry (bucket small IO sizes; owner: Ethan).
3) Add a canary trial: enable warm-mode for 5% of traffic for 48h to validate cost / latency tradeoffs (owner: Priya).

Medium-term (1–3 months):
- Investigate stripe-aware allocation: place pages from the same logical cluster across different NVMe lanes to avoid single-lane saturation. Needs cross-stack infra changes (owner: infra team engagement).
- Improve prefetch prediction model using short-run sequence prefix (ML model to decide prefetch distance based on first N tokens of request). Prototype with offline traces first (owner: applied-ml).

Operational runbook snippets (for SRE / on-call):
- If p99 > 300 ms and NVMe read throughput > 3 GB/s for > 20s: temporarily scale out hosts and enable per-host warm-mode via admin toggle.
- If warm-mode causes memory pressure > 90% for > 60s: roll back warm-mode and investigate which tenants are causing pressure.

Open questions / experiment ideas:
- Would coalescing small reads at block layer (align pages to 256KB windows) materially reduce tail latency? Risk: read amplification if we fetch too many pages.
- Can we detect cluster shifts at router-level (request routing) earlier, before evaporable keys are evicted?
- How do multi-tenant interplay and noisy neighbors change the thresholds?

Appendix: commands & snippets used in lab
- resident snapshot: /opt/redwood/bin/resident-snapshot --interval=10 --out=/tmp/res-snap.json
- per-request trace collection (local debug): ./trace_collect --req-log /tmp/reqs.log --kv-hits /tmp/hits.log
- simple fio to approximate NVMe behavior: fio --name=seq-read --rw=read --bs=4k --iodepth=16 --numjobs=4 --size=10G --runtime=60 --direct=1

Action items next sprint:
- [Priya] Roll out telemetry histogram change (2w).
- [Marco] PR for warm-mode basic implementation + feature flag (3w).
- [Lina] Prototype short-prefix prefetcher offline and test cost model (6w).
- [Ethan] Run stripe-saturation microbench with infra to validate multi-lane allocations (4w).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working lab note; lots of rough numbers. Please comment with any additional signals we should capture in the next runs (e.g., NVMe queue depth per process, per-host PCIe counters if available).

-- end --
